extracted.intended_audience: readers interested in political economy, legislators, policymakers, and educated public
extracted.subtask_description: Normative guidance for how a civil society should organize education, military exercises, religious institutions, and incentives to promote useful instruction and public order. The page gives prescriptions for school organization, teacher payment, militia practice, clergy provision, and remedies for fanaticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essential education for the common people (read, write, account)
rubrics_metrics.description: The most essential parts of education, however, to read, write, and account, can be acquired at so early a period of life, that the greater part, even of those who are to be bred to the lowest occupations, have time to acquire them before they can be employed in those occupations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The public can facilitate this acquisition by establishing in every parish or district a little school, where children may be taught for a reward so moderate that even a common labourer may afford it; the master being partly, but not wholly, paid by the public. Scotland's parish schools and English charity schools are offered as examples of this effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Payment model for schoolmasters (partly public, not wholly)
rubrics_metrics.description: The master being partly, but not wholly, paid by the public; because, if he was wholly, or even principally, paid by it, he would soon learn to neglect his business.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If masters were wholly salaried by the state they'd likely become negligent. Public support should be partial to preserve teachers' industry and accountability to pupils and parents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical curriculum for common schools (geometry and mechanics over Latin)
rubrics_metrics.description: If, instead of a little smattering in Latin, which the children of the common people are sometimes taught, and which can scarce ever be of any use to them, they were instructed in the elementary parts of geometry and mechanics; the literary education of this rank of people would, perhaps, be as complete as can be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elementary geometry and mechanics are relevant because almost every common trade affords opportunities to apply those principles; they would exercise and improve the understanding and introduce apprentices to useful sciences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public incentives for scholastic excellence (premiums and badges)
rubrics_metrics.description: The public can encourage the acquisition of those most essential parts of education, by giving small premiums, and little badges of distinction, to the children of the common people who excel in them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use modest rewards and visible marks of distinction to motivate learners in lower ranks; analogous to prizes in athletic or civic contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compulsory probation/examination before trade or corporate freedom
rubrics_metrics.description: The public can impose upon almost the whole body of the people the necessity of acquiring the most essential parts of education, by obliging every man to undergo an examination or probation in them, before he can obtain the freedom in any corporation, or be allowed to set up any trade.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Making certification a precondition for economic participation ensures broad uptake of basic literacy and numeracy among those entering trades or guilds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public facilitation of military/gymnastic exercises (simple, public institutions)
rubrics_metrics.description: They facilitated the acquisition of those exercises by appointing a certain place for learning and practising them, and by granting to certain masters the privilege of teaching in that place. Those masters do not appear to have had either salaries or exclusive privileges of any kind. Their reward consisted altogether in what they got from their scholars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ancient public gymnasia were simple, self-executing institutions requiring little government attention; modern complex militia regulations are prone to neglect and disuse without continual government effort. Simplicity and universality make such institutions durable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of prizes and public honors to sustain martial spirit
rubrics_metrics.description: Those republics encouraged the acquisition of those exercises by bestowing little premiums and badges of distinction upon those who excelled in them. To have gained a prize in the Olympic, Isthmian, or Nemaean games, gave illustration, not only to the person who gained it, but to his whole family and kindred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public competitions and honors stimulate participation and maintain civic virtues; rewards attach social prestige to competence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of universal martial spirit versus standing army
rubrics_metrics.description: Where every citizen had the spirit of a soldier, a smaller standing army would surely be requisite. That spirit, besides, would necessarily diminish very much the dangers to liberty, whether real or imaginary, which are commonly apprehended from a standing army.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A broadly martial citizenry reduces reliance on large standing forces and lessens the risk that standing armies could be used against constitutional liberty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer voluntary provision for clergy to stimulate zeal (with caveats)
rubrics_metrics.description: The teachers of the doctrine may either depend altogether for their subsistence upon the voluntary contributions of their hearers; or they may derive it from some other fund... Their exertion, their zeal and industry, are likely to be much greater in the former situation than in the latter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Voluntary support tends to keep inferior clergy energetic and zealous (examples: mendicant orders, parochial clergy drawing voluntary oblations); however, voluntary dependence can incentivize practices that exploit credulity and passion, leading to superstition and fanaticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dangers of interested diligence among clergy (perversion of truth)
rubrics_metrics.description: This interested diligence of the clergy is what every wise legislator will study to prevent; because, in every religion except the true, it is highly pernicious, and it has even a natural tendency to pervert the truth, by infusing into it a strong mixture of superstition, folly, and delusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When clergy depend on attracting retainers for subsistence they may pander to passions, vilify other sects, and adopt novelties to excite devotion. The legislator must guard against excessive commercialized zeal in spiritual matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political consequence of establishing or favouring one religion
rubrics_metrics.description: If politics had never called in the aid of religion, the sovereign would probably have dealt equally and impartially with all the different sects... but where there is an established or governing religion, the sovereign can in this case never be secure, unless he has the means of influencing in a considerable degree the greater part of the teachers of that religion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Established churches form incorporated bodies able to act concertedly and pursue interests sometimes opposed to the sovereign; political alliances between states and sects can lead to persecution of adversaries and to provision claims by clergy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal neutrality among sects fosters moderation and candour
rubrics_metrics.description: In a country where the law favoured the teachers of no one religion more than those of another, it would not be necessary that any of them should have any particular or immediate dependency upon the sovereign... the teachers of each little sect, finding themselves almost alone, would be obliged to learn that candour and moderation which are so seldom to be found among the teachers of those great sects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many small, competing sects reduce fanaticism because each teacher faces numerous adversaries; mutual concessions and the necessity of surviving among rivals tend to moderate doctrines toward more rational religion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedies for disagreeably rigorous morals of small sects
rubrics_metrics.description: Two easy and effectual remedies: (1) the study of science and philosophy (made almost universal among superior ranks, with probation for certain professions); (2) the frequency and gaiety of public diversions (painting, poetry, music, dancing, dramatic representations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 1) Require or encourage higher education/probation for those entering liberal professions to inoculate elites against enthusiasm and superstition. 2) Encourage public amusements to dissipate melancholy and break conditions favorable to fanaticism; dramatic representations expose artifice to ridicule and are particularly effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: State encouragement for callings that bring no private advantage
rubrics_metrics.description: There are some callings which, though useful and even necessary in a state, bring no advantage or pleasure to any individual; and the supreme power is obliged to alter its conduct with regard to the retainers of those professions. It must give them public encouragement in order to their subsistence; and it must provide against that negligence to which they will naturally be subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For professions like finance, fleets, and magistracy, the state should provide public encouragement, honours, or a system of ranks/subordination to secure their diligence because private incentives are insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk that independent provision becomes politically motivated
rubrics_metrics.description: Times of violent religious controversy have generally been times of equally violent political faction. Each political party has either found it, or imagined it, for his interest, to league itself with some one or other of the contending religious sects... Their first demand was generally that he should silence and subdue all their adversaries; and their second, that he should bestow an independent provision on themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provision for clergy is often sought as political spoil; legislators should be conscious that grants to religious groups can be intertwined with factional power and lead to demands for suppression of rivals and long-term political leverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clergy as an incorporated body (collective political power)
rubrics_metrics.description: The clergy of every established church constitute a great incorporation. They can act in concert, and pursue their interest upon one plan, and with one spirit as much as if they were under the direction of one man; and they are frequently, too, under such direction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the clergy can coordinate and pursue a corporate interest diverging from the sovereign's, governments with established churches must consider mechanisms to influence or moderate clerical power to maintain state security and policy aims.
